title: Beyond Best-of-𝑘: Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems

paper.title: Beyond Best-of- k k : Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of- k k runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems. †

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Measurement consistency is not sufficient for reconstruction. A single Fourier magnitude measurement is shared by rotations, translations, and color-channel inversions of an image. Existing solvers may return these prior-inconsistent modes, while PC-DAPS selects reconstructions supported by the learned image prior. Each sample was selected randomly, either from four independent runs for other methods or from the four particles generated in a single PC-DAPS run. Inverse problems arise across science and engineering whenever an unknown signal must be recovered from indirect measurements, including image restoration ( Bertero et al., 2021 ) , medical imaging ( Song et al., 2022 ) , and astronomical imaging ( Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, 2019 ) . Given an observed measurement y y generated through a known but potentially noisy measurement process, the goal of the inverse problem is to recover the original signal x x . For underdetermined problems, in which many different signals x x may give rise to the same measurement y y , Bayesian imaging defines the posterior distribution as p ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) ∝ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) ​ p ​ ( x ) p(x\mid y)\propto p(y\mid x)p(x) , where the likelihood p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) captures measurement consistency of a candidate image x x and the prior p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) captures which candidate reconstructions are plausible natural signals. The goal of posterior sampling is thus to generate candidate reconstructions that are simultaneously consistent with the measurement and the prior. In Fourier phase retrieval, for example, multiple images can produce identical Fourier magnitude measurements ( Fienup, 1982 ) . These measurement-equivalent solutions therefore have the same likelihood, but can have very different posterior probabilities depending on their consistency with the image prior. In particular, we observe that existing phase-retrieval solvers applied to face images sometimes return a rotated or color-inverted face that is consistent with the measurement but implausible under a natural-image prior concentrated on upright faces. The challenge is therefore not simply to find measurement-consistent reconstructions, but to sample the measurement-consistent solutions supported by the prior. Diffusion models provide strong image priors for posterior sampling ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . At each noise level, a diffusion model implicitly defines a denoiser that maps a noisy sample x t x_{t} to an estimate of the corresponding clean image; this diffusion denoiser can be used to incorporate the prior p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) during posterior sampling. Diffusion-based inverse solvers apply this prior information along a sampling trajectory , i.e., the sequence of intermediate states that evolves from a noisy sample toward a reconstruction. Existing methods primarily either tilt the unconditional reverse diffusion process using an approximate likelihood gradient ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boys et al., 2024 ) or alternate prior and measurement updates across noise levels ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Xu and Chi, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Ahmed and Makin, 2026 ) . In these methods, the prior information available at each noise level is represented through a local denoising approximation centered on a single clean-image estimate, rather than explicitly maintaining multiple competing prior modes at intermediate timesteps. When the measurement is ambiguous, as in the case of phase retrieval and other underdetermined inverse problems, following a sampling trajectory can lead to premature mode selection . At high noise levels, multiple prior modes may remain plausible, but the trajectory can only move towards one of them. Once a trajectory selects a particular prior mode, subsequent refinement primarily improves measurement consistency in the local neighborhood of that mode rather than considering more distant alternatives. This becomes problematic when (i) the selected prior mode is not consistent with the measurement, and (ii) its nearest measurement-consistent mode is not supported by the prior. Trajectory-based samplers can prematurely commit to this pair of modes, ultimately resulting in hallucinatory sampled reconstructions that are not supported by the true posterior or even the true prior. Best-of- k k evaluation partially masks this issue by generating multiple independent reconstructions and selecting the one closest to the ground truth ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . However, this selection uses information unavailable at test time and does not ensure that the produced samples are prior-consistent. Particle-based approaches maintain multiple candidates at intermediate timesteps ( Cardoso et al., 2024 ; Dou and Song, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) , but have primarily focused on linear inverse problems and particle diversity rather than prior-consistent sampling. To address this issue, we introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), which moves sample selection inside the sampler and removes the need for ground-truth-based best-of- k k evaluation. PC-DAPS maintains a bag of K K particles annealed under the same measurement, and models the denoiser posterior p ⁡ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) p(x_{0}\mid x_{t}) with a K K -component Gaussian mixture rather than a unimodal estimate. Early in sampling, multiple candidates are kept while the noise level is high and the prior is still weakly informative. As the noise decreases during annealing, particles with low prior consistency are pruned and replaced by surviving candidates that are more prior-consistent. PC-DAPS thus delays mode selection until the prior becomes more informative, performing within a single sampling run (and without ground-truth access) what best-of- k k does only after k k independent sampling runs. We evaluate PC-DAPS on FFHQ ( Karras et al., 2019 ) and ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) across three nonlinear and seven linear tasks, including the eight tasks reported in DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) as well as high-pass filtering ( Thaker et al., 2025 ) and 16 × \times super-resolution. We report PSNR, SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) under both single-sample and best-of- k k evaluation. We additionally compare the rate of prior-inconsistent hallucinations against independent DAPS runs. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves performance on ambiguous nonlinear problems while maintaining image quality and diversity on linear inverse problems. Our contributions are as follows: • We propose PC-DAPS, which maintains a bag of particles, models the denoiser posterior with a Gaussian mixture, and performs prior-based pruning without access to ground truth. • We evaluate PC-DAPS across seven linear and three nonlinear inverse problems on FFHQ and ImageNet, showing fewer prior-inconsistent reconstructions and improved nonlinear reconstruction quality while preserving performance on linear tasks.

In contrast, variable-splitting methods alternate between prior-only and measurement-only steps. Among methods using a diffusion model for the prior step, PnP-DM ( Wu et al., 2024 ) uses a split Gibbs sampler for the likelihood, while DPnP ( Xu and Chi, 2024 ) uses Metropolis-Hastings and DiffPIR ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) utilizes a proximal step. RePS ( Ahmed and Makin, 2026 ) adds restarts to that schedule, and DAPS++ ( Chen et al., 2026 ) reports that the DAPS reconstruction is largely driven by measurement consistency. We therefore design PC-DAPS as a modification of DAPS that retains its variable-splitting structure but introduces prior-based selection to discriminate between measurement-consistent reconstructions. Particle-based posterior sampling. Another group of approaches maintains many particles throughout sampling, and uses sequential Monte Carlo to propagate, reweight, and resample particles to progressively improve measurement consistency ( Cardoso et al., 2024 ; Janati et al., 2025 ) . FPS-SMC ( Dou and Song, 2024 ) casts the reverse sampling process as a state-space model and applies a particle filter. TDS ( Wu et al., 2023 ) uses twisting functions to obtain asymptotic exactness for general measurement models. While particle-based methods are typically concerned with the fidelity of the ensemble in the limit of many particles, we are concerned instead with the probability that a single returned reconstruction is prior-inconsistent, and use particles for the purpose of exploring the posterior landscape. Diagnosing hallucination and prior misfit. Hallucination has been studied as a property of reconstruction algorithms in inverse problems since before diffusion priors were adopted ( Bhadra et al., 2021 ) , and refers to any reconstruction that is inconsistent with either the measurement or the prior. Recent work has sought to quantify hallucination specifically for diffusion-based solvers ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . At the level of the model rather than the individual sample, DiME ( Wang and Bouman, 2026 ) estimates the evidence of a diffusion prior by integrating over the time-marginals of a posterior sampler, and can be run alongside DAPS to detect prior misfit. Closest to our framing, Burns and Fridovich-Keil (2026) adopt a finite-sample perspective on reverse diffusion dynamics and show that widely used guidance approximations misestimate posterior spread at intermediate noise levels. This misestimation produces both prior modes absent from the true posterior and likelihood (measurement-consistent) modes unsupported by the prior, which is the specific failure that our PC-DAPS method aims to address. Benchmarks whose posteriors are analytically tractable provide a complementary check on the uncertainty a solver reports ( Crafts and Villa, 2025 ; Zach et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . All of these existing hallucination diagnostics are applied after sampling; PC-DAPS utilizes prior support during sampling to decide which reconstructions survive, thereby reducing the incidence of prior-inconsistent hallucinations.

sections.text: We consider Bayesian inverse problems of the form: y = 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) + n , n ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , β y 2 ​ I ) , y=\mathcal{A}(x)+n,\qquad n\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\beta_{y}^{2}I), (1) where x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the unknown signal of interest, 𝒜 : ℝ d → ℝ m \mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} is a known measurement operator that is deterministic but may be linear or nonlinear, n ∈ ℝ m n\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is unknown additive Gaussian noise, and y ∈ ℝ m y\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is the observed measurement. Given a prior distribution p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) , Bayes’ rule gives the posterior distribution over likely signals x x consistent with a provided measurement y y : p ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) ∝ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) ​ p ​ ( x ) , p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( y , 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) , β y 2 ​ I ) . p(x\mid y)\propto p(y\mid x)\,p(x),\qquad p(y\mid x)=\mathcal{N}\bigl(y;\mathcal{A}(x),\beta_{y}^{2}I\bigr). (2) We are particularly interested in forward models where the set of measurement-consistent signals ℳ ⁡ ( y ) = { x ∈ ℝ d : ‖ 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) − y ‖ ≤ δ } \mathcal{M}(y)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|\mathcal{A}(x)-y\|\leq\delta\right\} (3) contains multiple candidate reconstructions which are well-separated in signal space. In this context, two distinct signals in ℳ ⁡ ( y ) \mathcal{M}(y) can be assigned equal likelihoods p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) but have drastically different posterior probabilities p ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) p(x\mid y) , as one image might be unrealistic (i.e., significantly lower prior probability p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) ). A common failure case of existing reconstruction methods is to sample both signals with roughly equal frequency, thereby misrepresenting their posterior probabilities as relatively equal. For example, in Fourier phase retrieval, two images which are identical up to rotation, translation, and/or color channel sign appear visually quite distinct but produce identical Fourier magnitude measurements ( Fienup, 1982 ) . On structured face images, a solver can return a 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} -rotated or color-inverted (e.g., blue) face that fits the observed Fourier measurement despite being inconsistent with a prior distribution supported only on the set of upright faces. We refer to such reconstructions as prior-inconsistent . Prior-inconsistent reconstructions commonly appear across classical phase-retrieval methods ( Fienup, 1982 ) , deep-learning approaches ( Metzler et al., 2018 ; Işil and Oktem, 2025 ) , and diffusion-based inverse-problem solvers ( Xu and Chi, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Our goal is to reduce the frequency of prior-inconsistent solutions while retaining quality and diversity of measurement- and prior-consistent samples.

Figure 2 illustrates this phenomenon. Here, the prior places mass on two candidate solutions, x 1 x_{1} and x 2 x_{2} , while the measurement y y is explained by x 1 x_{1} and a third point x 3 x_{3} unsupported by the prior. In analogy to Fourier phase retrieval, one can think of x 1 x_{1} as the desired reconstruction, e.g., an upright, non-blue face that is both consistent with the measurement and supported by the image prior, x 2 x_{2} as a realistic face inconsistent with the particular measurement, and x 3 x_{3} as a structurally implausible transformation of the desired image x 1 x_{1} , such as a rotated or blue face. The exact posterior should favor the x 1 x_{1} mode while assigning zero mass to the prior-inconsistent x 3 x_{3} . However, DAPS samples from x 3 x_{3} ’s neighborhood by (i) sampling x 2 x_{2} from the prior and (ii) sampling x 3 x_{3} from x 2 x_{2} ’s local likelihood. Once a particle enters this locally attractive likelihood-consistent region, subsequent renoising and Langevin updates become trapped, resulting in premature mode selection. This toy example motivates the design of PC-DAPS, which maintains multiple candidate measurement-consistent modes to identify and correct trapped prior-inconsistent samples. As shown in Figure 2 , PC-DAPS places its mass only on the prior-supported and measurement-consistent mode at x 1 x_{1} and avoids sampling from the prior-inconsistent, measurement-consistent region near x 3 x_{3} . We describe how PC-DAPS identifies and removes such prior-inconsistent particles in the next section.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: To address the presence of prior-inconsistent samples, a first approach might be to produce multiple samples via DAPS and discard any which are prior-inconsistent. There are two main shortcomings of this approach: (i) the effective sample size of this sampling method is suboptimal, as substantial computational resources are used to produce samples that are then thrown out, and (ii) it is unclear how to select which samples to discard without having access to the ground truth signal or posterior. To address these issues, we introduce PC-DAPS, a procedure for correcting prematurely committed particles during the sampling process without requiring access to the ground truth image or to any pre-trained prior-inconsistency classifier. PC-DAPS maintains a bag of K K particles, each of which is denoised using the same annealing schedule and pretrained denoiser, but uses different initializations and random noise in its Langevin and renoising updates. If no additional modifications are made to DAPS, the K K particles will denoise independently, and can be partitioned into (nonempty) sets of “bad” prematurely committed particles and “good” particles that are posterior-consistent. The core idea of PC-DAPS is to improve DAPS’s existing renoising strategy by identifying prematurely committed particles during sampling and moving them to more promising modes discovered by other particles in the bag. Additionally, PC-DAPS utilizes the particles to refine additional design decisions made by DAPS, such as by replacing the unimodal Gaussian approximation to the denoising distribution with an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM) approximation. A toy example illustrating the benefit of this Gaussian mixture approximation is shown in Section A.3 . What remains is to describe how PC-DAPS (i) identifies when particles commit prematurely, (ii) identifies which particles are problematic, (iii) corrects the identified particles, and (iv) constructs the multimodal denoising distribution approximation from the bag. PC-DAPS makes two core changes to DAPS, utilizing K K particles annealed in parallel: a pruning technique to correct particles trapped in prior-inconsistent likelihood modes in tasks with likelihood ambiguity ( Section 4.1 ), and a multimodal denoising distribution approximation estimated from the diversity of the particles ( Section 4.2 ). Additional implementation details and ablations are provided in Section A.4 , such as omitting the final Langevin refinement and adaptive ODE stepping from high to low noise to improve reconstruction quality while reducing computational cost ( Section A.5 ). The full algorithm ( Algorithm 1 ) can be found in Section A.1 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Gaussian mixture approximation of the denoiser posterior
sections.text: An additional benefit of maintaining a bag of particles is that we can improve upon DAPS’s unimodal approximation in Equation 6 by selecting a multimodal distribution informed by the bag’s diversity. sections.heading: Prior-inconsistent hallucinations.
sections.text: Table 1 reports standard metrics to facilitate baseline comparisons. However, the evaluation procedure masks the failure mode PC-DAPS aims to address (measurement-consistent reconstructions that the prior does not support), because the best-of- k k evaluation protocol used by baseline methods discards k − 1 k-1 of the reconstructed images. On phase retrieval, we instead classify every sample as faithful , upside-down / color-inverted (a measurement-consistent likelihood mode the natural-image prior would down-weight), or failed . Labels are assigned automatically using per-channel PSNR to the ground truth and its rotated version, maximizing over ± 1 \pm 1 -pixel circular shifts to account for translation ambiguity. A channel is assigned to an orientation only when it is more than 1 1 dB closer to that orientation; samples with all channels matching the ground truth are faithful , those matching the rotation or disagreeing across channels are upside-down / color-inverted , and the remainder are failed . When the local geometry of the prior support is more complex, data-manifold-based prior-consistency pruning appears to be less effective.

sections.heading: Motivation, limitations, and future work.
sections.text: Results in the diffusion literature for ambiguous inverse problems are usually reported as best-of- k k , with selection using the ground truth. This evaluation approach became common because existing solvers are inconsistent across runs, and a single-sample result would have large variations in quality. We see this instability as a symptom of premature mode selection in the context of measurement ambiguity. We introduce PC-DAPS to utilize the learned prior information to reduce this unwanted variance during sampling without the need for a ground-truth reference. Even in high-dimensional datasets, including FFHQ, our method demonstrates significant improvements due to the local structure of the prior. PC-DAPS obtains a smaller improvement on more structurally diverse datasets, namely ImageNet, because the prior landscape is more complex, exposing a remaining limitation and open problem to be addressed. We encourage future work to further explore our proposed paradigm of leveraging the prior score to assess candidate reconstructions at inference time, and work towards eliminating prior-inconsistent reconstructions even under less-structured priors.

sections.heading: Posterior sampling metrics.
sections.text: Standard metrics like PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS measure how similar a generated image is to a single reference image. Observe that these evaluation metrics penalize methods that find several plausible solutions that are equally valid under the measurement and prior if the solutions are dissimilar from the fixed reference. Because sample diversity and likelihood consistency are explicit goals of posterior sampling, including in applications such as uncertainty quantification, these sample-quality metrics are not adequate replacements for quality of the sampled posterior. In our work, we report a separate axis of reconstruction quality: prior consistency. We believe this or similar multifaceted metrics should be considered alongside standard fidelity metrics.

sections.heading: A.4 Additional implementation choices
sections.text: There are two implementation choices that are orthogonal to the core PC-DAPS algorithm but improve reconstruction quality or computational efficiency in practice: skipping the final Langevin refinement and using adaptive ODE stepping. Their effects are summarized in Table 3 and described in detail below.

sections.heading: Skipping the last Langevin refinement.
sections.text: At the final annealing time ( t 0 = 0 t_{0}=0 ), the Langevin update is not performed, and the ODE endpoint x ^ 0 ​ ( x t 0 ) \hat{x}_{0}(x_{t_{0}}) is used as the output. When the noise is nearly zero, the Langevin step size becomes very small, and the added noise can slightly reduce sample quality.

sections.heading: Adaptive ODE steps.
sections.text: To compute the DAPS clean estimate x ^ 0 ​ ( x t i ) \hat{x}_{0}(x_{t_{i}}) , the probability flow ODE is integrated using Euler steps. One Euler step is used at high noise levels, where the clean estimate is less sensitive to the precise ODE integration, and this is increased to five steps at lower noise levels, where the prior becomes more discriminative and finer integration reduces discretization error near the data manifold. Since PC-DAPS utilizes a bag of multiple particles, reducing unnecessary ODE evaluations is important for controlling the additional computational cost. Adaptive ODE stepping is therefore used to improve the time efficiency of the particle-based sampler. Descriptions of the implementation details of the particle clustering and pruning procedure used by PC-DAPS are given below.

sections.heading: Clustering technique.
sections.text: To assign particles to components, the corresponding clean samples { x ~ 0 ( k ) } k = 1 K \{\tilde{x}_{0}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} described in Section 4.2 are downsampled to a coarse resolution (e.g., 32 × 32 32{\times}32 ), centered, and projected onto the leading principal components that explain 90 % 90\% of the variance. On this subspace, a Gaussian mixture model is fit with M M selected via Bayesian information criterion ( Schwarz, 1978 ) . Each particle is then hard-assigned to its most likely component, giving a partition { 𝒞 m } m = 1 M \{\mathcal{C}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} of the bag.

sections.heading: A.5 Time cost
sections.text: PC-DAPS keeps K K particles in one sampling trajectory, while DAPS needs K K separate runs to get K K candidate reconstructions. If implementation overhead is ignored, both methods need about the same number of denoiser evaluations, which increases roughly linearly with K K . PC-DAPS does have extra steps, including clustering, estimating mixture parameters, and a one-shot pruning step. However, these add only a small overhead compared to the cost of the ODE and Langevin updates. The implementation choices in Section A.4 , such as skipping the final Langevin refinement and using adaptive ODE steps at low noise, help lower the sampling cost of PC-DAPS. Figure 8 shows the measured wall-clock time and reconstruction quality. For super-resolution, PC-DAPS takes longer than DAPS because it uses multiple particles. For phase retrieval, though, the DAPS runtime includes four separate runs because it uses a best-of-4 evaluation protocol. PC-DAPS, on the other hand, creates the particle set in one run and selects internally. These results suggest that using multiple particles does not always mean a much higher wall-clock cost to achieve the same quality metric. sections.heading: A.6 Inverse problem setup
sections.text: In Table 1 , following the inverse-problem settings of DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , the benchmark includes the eight tasks from DAPS: 4 × 4{\times} super-resolution, box inpainting, random inpainting, Gaussian deblurring, motion deblurring, nonlinear deblurring, phase retrieval, and high dynamic range (HDR) reconstruction. For these tasks, the same measurement operators, measurement noise level, and evaluation protocol as DAPS are used. Unless otherwise stated, measurements are corrupted with additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation β y = 0.05 \beta_{y}=0.05 . Methods are evaluated on 100 test images from each dataset, FFHQ and ImageNet, at a resolution of 256 × 256 256{\times}256 . Additionally, 16 × 16{\times} super-resolution and high-pass filtering from Thaker et al. (2025) are included in the table and described in detail below.

sections.heading: Super-resolution 16 × 16{\times} .
sections.text: Bicubic downsampling is applied from 256 × 256 256{\times}256 to 16 × 16 16{\times}16 , followed by additive Gaussian noise with standard deviation β y = 0.05 \beta_{y}=0.05 . This uses the same linear bicubic downsampling operator as the 4 × 4{\times} super-resolution task in DAPS, but with a larger downsampling factor. The resulting operator has a larger null space, leaving more image content unconstrained by the measurement and providing a more challenging setting. All other sampler settings follow the 4 × 4{\times} super-resolution configuration.

sections.heading: High-pass filtering.
sections.text: Following Thaker et al. (2025) , a 61 × 61 61{\times}61 convolutional kernel is used, constructed as a Dirac delta minus a Gaussian blur kernel with standard deviation 5.0 5.0 . The resulting kernel has zero sum and therefore removes the DC component. Gaussian noise with standard deviation β y = 0.05 \beta_{y}=0.05 is added to the filtered image.

Burns 4* Andreas Geiger 1,5,6,7 Kent Gauen 4 Sara Fridovich-Keil 4 1 University of Tübingen 2 Zuse School ELIZA 3 Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems 4 Georgia Institute of Technology 5 Tübingen AI Center 6 ELLIS Institute 7 KE:SAI * Equal contribution merve.kocabas@student.uni-tuebingen.de a.geiger@uni-tuebingen.de {bburns46,gauenk,sfk}@gatech.edu Abstract Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of- k k runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems. † †\dagger † †\dagger † \dagger Code: https://github.com/voilalab/PC-DAPS ; project website: PC-DAPS . 1 Introduction Figure 1: Measurement consistency is not sufficient for reconstruction. A single Fourier magnitude measurement is shared by rotations, translations, and color-channel inversions of an image. Existing solvers may return these prior-inconsistent modes, while PC-DAPS selects reconstructions supported by the learned image prior. Each sample was selected randomly, either from four independent runs for other methods or from the four particles generated in a single PC-DAPS run. Inverse problems arise across science and engineering whenever an unknown signal must be recovered from indirect measurements, including image restoration ( Bertero et al., 2021 ) , medical imaging ( Song et al., 2022 ) , and astronomical imaging ( Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, 2019 ) . Given an observed measurement y y generated through a known but potentially noisy measurement process, the goal of the inverse problem is to recover the original signal x x . For underdetermined problems, in which many different signals x x may give rise to the same measurement y y , Bayesian imaging defines the posterior distribution as p ⁡ ( x ∣ y ) ∝ p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) ​ p ​ ( x ) p(x\mid y)\propto p(y\mid x)p(x) , where the likelihood p ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) p(y\mid x) captures measurement consistency of a candidate image x x and the prior p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) captures which candidate reconstructions are plausible natural signals. The goal of posterior sampling is thus to generate candidate reconstructions that are simultaneously consistent with the measurement and the prior. In Fourier phase retrieval, for example, multiple images can produce identical Fourier magnitude measurements ( Fienup, 1982 ) . These measurement-equivalent solutions therefore have the same likelihood, but can have very different posterior probabilities depending on their consistency with the image prior. In particular, we observe that existing phase-retrieval solvers applied to face images sometimes return a rotated or color-inverted face that is consistent with the measurement but implausible under a natural-image prior concentrated on upright faces. The challenge is therefore not simply to find measurement-consistent reconstructions, but to sample the measurement-consistent solutions supported by the prior. Diffusion models provide strong image priors for posterior sampling ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . At each noise level, a diffusion model implicitly defines a denoiser that maps a noisy sample x t x_{t} to an estimate of the corresponding clean image; this diffusion denoiser can be used to incorporate the prior p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) during posterior sampling. Diffusion-based inverse solvers apply this prior information along a sampling trajectory , i.e., the sequence of intermediate states that evolves from a noisy sample toward a reconstruction. Existing methods primarily either tilt the unconditional reverse diffusion process using an approximate likelihood gradient ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Boys et al., 2024 ) or alternate prior and measurement updates across noise levels ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Xu and Chi, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Ahmed and Makin, 2026 ) . In these methods, the prior information available at each noise level is represented through a local denoising approximation centered on a single clean-image estimate, rather than explicitly maintaining multiple competing prior modes at intermediate timesteps. When the measurement is ambiguous, as in the case of phase retrieval and other underdetermined inverse problems, following a sampling trajectory can lead to premature mode selection . At high noise levels, multiple prior modes may remain plausible, but the trajectory can only move towards one of them. Once a trajectory selects a particular prior mode, subsequent refinement primarily improves measurement consistency in the local neighborhood of that mode rather than considering more distant alternatives. This becomes problematic when (i) the selected prior mode is not consistent with the measurement, and (ii) its nearest measurement-consistent mode is not supported by the prior. Trajectory-based samplers can prematurely commit to this pair of modes, ultimately resulting in hallucinatory sampled reconstructions that are not supported by the true posterior or even the true prior. Best-of- k k evaluation partially masks this issue by generating multiple independent reconstructions and selecting the one closest to the ground truth ( Chung et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . However, this selection uses information unavailable at test time and does not ensure that the produced samples are prior-consistent. Particle-based approaches maintain multiple candidates at intermediate timesteps ( Cardoso et al., 2024 ; Dou and Song, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) , but have primarily focused on linear inverse problems and particle diversity rather than prior-consistent sampling. To address this issue, we introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), which moves sample selection inside the sampler and removes the need for ground-truth-based best-of- k k evaluation. PC-DAPS maintains a bag of K K particles annealed under the same measurement, and models the denoiser posterior p ⁡ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) p(x_{0}\mid x_{t}) with a K K -component Gaussian mixture rather than a unimodal estimate. Early in sampling, multiple candidates are kept while the noise level is high and the prior is still weakly informative. As the noise decreases during annealing, particles with low prior consistency are pruned and replaced by surviving candidates that are more prior-consistent. PC-DAPS thus delays mode selection until the prior becomes more informative, performing within a single sampling run (and without ground-truth access) what best-of- k k does only after k k independent sampling runs. We evaluate PC-DAPS on FFHQ ( Karras et al., 2019 ) and ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) across three nonlinear and seven linear tasks, including the eight tasks reported in DAPS ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) as well as high-pass filtering ( Thaker et al., 2025 ) and 16 × 	imes super-resolution. We report PSNR, SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) under both single-sample and best-of- k k evaluation. We additionally compare the rate of prior-inconsistent hallucinations against independent DAPS runs. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves performance on ambiguous nonlinear problems while maintaining image quality and diversity on linear inverse problems. RePS ( Ahmed and Makin, 2026 ) adds restarts to that schedule, and DAPS++ ( Chen et al., 2026 ) reports that the DAPS reconstruction is largely driven by measurement consistency. We therefore design PC-DAPS as a modification of DAPS that retains its variable-splitting structure but introduces prior-based selection to discriminate between measurement-consistent reconstructions. Particle-based posterior sampling. Another group of approaches maintains many particles throughout sampling, and uses sequential Monte Carlo to propagate, reweight, and resample particles to progressively improve measurement consistency ( Cardoso et al., 2024 ; Janati et al., 2025 ) . FPS-SMC ( Dou and Song, 2024 ) casts the reverse sampling process as a state-space model and applies a particle filter. TDS ( Wu et al., 2023 ) uses twisting functions to obtain asymptotic exactness for general measurement models. While particle-based methods are typically concerned with the fidelity of the ensemble in the limit of many particles, we are concerned instead with the probability that a single returned reconstruction is prior-inconsistent, and use particles for the purpose of exploring the posterior landscape. Diagnosing hallucination and prior misfit. Hallucination has been studied as a property of reconstruction algorithms in inverse problems since before diffusion priors were adopted ( Bhadra et al., 2021 ) , and refers to any reconstruction that is inconsistent with either the measurement or the prior. Recent work has sought to quantify hallucination specifically for diffusion-based solvers ( Jin et al., 2026 ) . At the level of the model rather than the individual sample, DiME ( Wang and Bouman, 2026 ) estimates the evidence of a diffusion prior by integrating over the time-marginals of a posterior sampler, and can be run alongside DAPS to detect prior misfit. Closest to our framing, Burns and Fridovich-Keil (2026) adopt a finite-sample perspective on reverse diffusion dynamics and show that widely used guidance approximations misestimate posterior spread at intermediate noise levels. This misestimation produces both prior modes absent from the true posterior and likelihood (measurement-consistent) modes unsupported by the prior, which is the specific failure that our PC-DAPS method aims to address. Benchmarks whose posteriors are analytically tractable provide a complementary check on the uncertainty a solver reports ( Crafts and Villa, 2025 ; Zach et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . All of these existing hallucination diagnostics are applied after sampling; PC-DAPS utilizes prior support during sampling to decide which reconstructions survive, thereby reducing the incidence of prior-inconsistent hallucinations. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Bayesian inverse problems We consider Bayesian inverse problems of the form: y = 𝒜 ⁡ ( x ) + n , n ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , β y 2 ​ I ) , y=\mathcal{A}(x)+n,\qquad n\sim\mathcal{N}(0, eta_{y}^{2}I), (1) where x ∈ ℝ d x\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the unknown signal of interest, 𝒜 : ℝ d → ℝ m \mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^{d}	o\mathbb{R}^{m} is a known measurement operator that is deterministic but may be linear or nonlinear, n ∈ ℝ m n\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is unknown additive Gaussian noise, and y ∈ ℝ m y\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is the observed measurement. There are two main shortcomings of this approach: (i) the effective sample size of this sampling method is suboptimal, as substantial computational resources are used to produce samples that are then thrown out, and (ii) it is unclear how to select which samples to discard without having access to the ground truth signal or posterior. To address these issues, we introduce PC-DAPS, a procedure for correcting prematurely committed particles during the sampling process without requiring access to the ground truth image or to any pre-trained prior-inconsistency classifier. PC-DAPS maintains a bag of K K particles, each of which is denoised using the same annealing schedule and pretrained denoiser, but uses different initializations and random noise in its Langevin and renoising updates. If no additional modifications are made to DAPS, the K K particles will denoise independently, and can be partitioned into (nonempty) sets of “bad” prematurely committed particles and “good” particles that are posterior-consistent. The core idea of PC-DAPS is to improve DAPS’s existing renoising strategy by identifying prematurely committed particles during sampling and moving them to more promising modes discovered by other particles in the bag. Additionally, PC-DAPS utilizes the particles to refine additional design decisions made by DAPS, such as by replacing the unimodal Gaussian approximation to the denoising distribution with an adaptive Gaussian mixture model (GMM) approximation. A toy example illustrating the benefit of this Gaussian mixture approximation is shown in Section A.3 . What remains is to describe how PC-DAPS (i) identifies when particles commit prematurely, (ii) identifies which particles are problematic, (iii) corrects the identified particles, and (iv) constructs the multimodal denoising distribution approximation from the bag. PC-DAPS makes two core changes to DAPS, utilizing K K particles annealed in parallel: a pruning technique to correct particles trapped in prior-inconsistent likelihood modes in tasks with likelihood ambiguity ( Section 4.1 ), and a multimodal denoising distribution approximation estimated from the diversity of the particles ( Section 4.2 ). Additional implementation details and ablations are provided in Section A.4 , such as omitting the final Langevin refinement and adaptive ODE stepping from high to low noise to improve reconstruction quality while reducing computational cost ( Section A.5 ).
